# [Week FOUR]{.r-fit-text}

Part III of @Hornbaek2025

*Interviews · Field Research · Surveys*

# Intro

For three weeks we've been building a general model of the human — perception, motor control, cognition, motivation. That model is powerful, but it's patchy: it tells you people satisfice and hate latency; it does not tell you what *your* users do on a Tuesday.

This week's question: *you are not your user, so how do you find out who is, and what they do?*

# Case Study: Quibi

<!-- IMAGE: Quibi app on a phone in portrait/landscape "Turnstyle" split, or the launch-day press image -->

# Why did Quibi fail?

$1.75 billion, Hollywood's best content, and a shutdown six months after launch.

- They asked people *"would you watch premium short-form video on your phone?"* — and people said yes. Classic **say–do gap**: stated preference, not observed behavior
- They designed for a **context** — commutes, coffee lines, in-between moments — and launched into April 2020, when nobody had one. Context isn't a backdrop; it's a variable
- They built for the founders' taste and the survey deck, not for observed practice: no screenshots, no sharing, no TV casting — every behavior users *actually* exhibited with mobile video was blocked
- The one-line model clash: leadership's model was *TV, but shorter*; users' model was *TikTok, but worse*

::: {.callout-tip title="In the wild"}
🎤 *A time your team (or a team you watched) shipped something because a survey or an exec said users wanted it — and the logs told a different story within a month. The specific shape: what people SAID vs. what the data SHOWED, and what it cost to find out the expensive way.*
:::

<!-- ~4 min -->

# You Are Not the User

## Why user research exists

- **You are not the user** — designers and developers are systematically unrepresentative; basing decisions on your own opinion is a bias, not a shortcut
- **Say–do gap** — what users say diverges from what they do; self-reported internet use correlates poorly with logged use, and a recent meta-analysis (**Parry et al., 2021**) puts self-report/log agreement at only moderate levels
- **Tacit knowledge** — much of what drives behavior can't be articulated (**Polanyi**): ask someone how they type their password and watch them fail to explain
- **Future blindness** — users can't articulate needs for technology they haven't experienced; no batch-computing user asked for a GUI
- **Work is kept invisible** — **Suchman (1995)**: making work practices visible can shift power in an organization, so people hide them

## What do we gather knowledge about?

- **PACT** (**Benyon**): **People** (skills, motivations, beliefs), **Activities** (what they actually do), **Contexts** (physical, social, organizational, historical, cultural), **Technologies** (what they use now)
- **Design-neutral descriptions** — understand first, design later; user research is applied empirical science, not brainstorming
- **The is–ought problem** — no description of what users *do* logically entails what you *should* build; data informs, it does not decide
- Research also **persuades**: a designer with interview data and models beats a designer with vibes in every stakeholder meeting

## Who counts as "the user"?

- Three steps, all failure-prone: define the **target audience** (behavioral, technological, demographic criteria) → identify **other stakeholders** → **sample**
- **Stakeholders** aren't users but are affected: **Mitchell et al. (1997)** — sort them by **power**, **legitimacy**, **urgency**; some are latent, some dormant (lawyers appear only after the accident)
- **Extreme users** (**Pullin & Newell, 2008**) — designing from the edges of ability distributions produced the tape recorder and easy-grip kitchen tools
- **Lead users** — early adopters with stronger needs preview the mainstream's future
- Defining the user is a **political decision**: are you designing for everyone, or for people who look like your managers?

# Choosing Methods

## No method is innocent

- **McGrath (1995)**: all methods are flawed; every choice trades off **realism** (is the situation like the real one?), **precision** (how exact is the measurement?), and **generalizability** (does it hold beyond this sample?)
- You cannot maximize all three — field studies buy realism at the cost of control; surveys buy generalizability at the cost of depth
- Methods differ on **open-ended vs. close-ended** (let the data speak vs. predefined categories) and **first-person vs. third-person** (ethnography vs. log analysis)
- Quibi callback: surveys were high-generalizability, zero-realism — and the question they answered wasn't the one that mattered

## Triangulation and quality

- **Triangulation** (**McGrath**): combine methods with *different* weaknesses so they compensate for each other — interviews + logs, surveys + observation
- Only about half of UX studies triangulate at all (**Pettersson et al., 2018**); the other half inherit one method's blind spots wholesale
- Four marks of methodological quality: **validity** (are the conclusions justified?), **reliability** (same result on repeat?), **transparency** (can others inspect the chain of evidence?), **ethics** (obligations to participants, clients, and society)

::: {.callout-warning title="Not so fast... is user research even worth it?"}
- The field treats "know the user" (**Hansen, 1971**) as an axiom, and ROI cases at HP were estimated at $6M–$125M per project (**Harper**)
- **Norman (2005)**, *Human-Centered Design Considered Harmful*, countered: chasing every user signal produces incoherent, feature-creeped systems — and users happily adapt to valuable tools that ignored them (the violin was not user-tested)
- Current consensus: user research reliably improves and de-risks designs; it rarely produces radical innovation on its own
- Design takeaway: treat user research as evidence that informs judgment — not as a requirements vending machine
:::

# Interviews Are a Craft

## Talking to people is not research

- Everyday conversation is unplanned, unrecorded, and aimed at rapport — not at understanding the other person's world; interviews are **systematic** conversation
- Three families: **structured** (fixed schedule — easy to run, easy to compare), **semi-structured / open-ended** (the HCI workhorse), **unstructured** (rare in HCI)
- Interviews access **beliefs, attitudes, experiences** — not frequencies; never interview to learn how *often* people do something (that's the say–do gap again)
- **Ames & Naaman (2007)** interviewed 13 Flickr users and overturned the assumption that tagging is self-promotion — people also tag for their own memory; two dimensions: sociality × function
- The stance: *"don't argue, never give advice"* — and listen more than you talk

## Question craft

- **Main questions** map to themes: tour ("walk me through..."), grounded ("the last file you downloaded..."), experience, comparison, stage questions
- **Probes** keep talk flowing ("tell me more", echoing their words); **follow-ups** deepen it (clarify, get concrete, compare, check variation)
- Kill **leading questions** ("How much did you like it?"), **double-barreled questions** (two topics, one question), and **judgmental wording**
- Ask about the **present, not the future** — "would you use X?" invites speculation; "is X useful to you right now?" invites evidence
- Use **"why?" sparingly** (**Rubin & Rubin**) — it demands justification, makes people defensive, and buys you a rationalization, not a reason

::: {.callout-tip title="In the wild"}
🎤 *A recording of (or story about) a real interview question that went wrong — ideally one of your own. The specific shape: the leading question as asked, the answer it produced, and the moment you realized the data was worthless.*
:::

## Contextual inquiry

- **Holtzblatt & Beyer**: watch users do work that matters to them *while* talking about it — interview woven into observation, 1.5–2 hours
- Four principles: **context** (be where the activity is), **partnership** (master–apprentice: the user does the talking), **interpretation** (build meaning together, listen for "no... but... maybe"), **focus** (go deep where the energy is)
- The killer probe: when they generalize ("I usually just..."), pull them back to the concrete — *"show me how"*, *"tell me about the last time"*
- This is the standard answer to tacit knowledge: what can't be said can often be **acted out**

## From talk to insight

- **Analysis expands meaning** (what did "liven up my feed" actually mean?) then **condenses it** (coding into patterns); do it soon after each interview, not at the end
- **Affinity diagramming** (**Kawakita's KJ method**; **Lucero, 2015**): notes → clusters → walk the wall → document; collaborative bottom-up coding
- **Thematic analysis** (**Braun & Clarke, 2006**): familiarize → code generously → generate themes → review → define → report; themes are *constructed* relative to your question, not found under a rock

::: {.callout-warning title="Not so fast... how many interviews are 'enough'?"}
- **Guest, Bunce & Johnson (2006)**: saturation arrived by ~12 interviews — cited thousands of times as a magic number
- **Braun & Clarke (2021)** countered: for reflexive thematic analysis, "saturation" is incoherent — meaning is generated by the analyst, so it can't run out; **Malterud et al. (2016)** propose "information power" instead
- Current consensus: sample size depends on question breadth, data richness, and analysis method — not a universal constant
- Design takeaway: never justify n=12 by citation alone; justify it by what your question needs
:::

# Into the Field

## Watching beats asking — sometimes

- **Field research** = collecting data on users in their real context; its superpower is **realism** — it captures what other methods structurally miss
- **Etic** observation: outsider's view, countable events, minimal interference. **Emic** (ethnography): insider's view, meanings and practices
- **MacKay (1999)** spent four months with air traffic controllers to understand their paper flight strips before a planned digitization — and found the paper *was* the safety system: cyclical checking, spatial arrangement, annotations "for the future"
- Field research excels at **discrepancy problems**: the gap between how managers think work happens and how it actually gets done

## Some paper that shouldn't be replaced

<!-- IMAGE: air traffic control paper flight strips arranged on a control board -->

## Doing observation well

- **Focus** is a decision, not a default: **Spradley (1980)** gives nine dimensions — space, actors, activities, objects, acts, events, time, goals, feelings
- **Site selection** shapes everything; orient with a floor plan; watch for **reactivity** — the observer changes the observed (imagine being shadowed by someone your boss hired)
- **Shadowing** follows people instead of places: **González & Mark (2004)** found workers average under 2.5 minutes on email before switching
- **Field notes** are the raw data: diaries are flexible but sporadic; **structured notes** enable patterns and counting; write **thick descriptions** fast — memory decays by lunch
- Coding needs a **manual** with unambiguous definitions, and **inter-rater reliability** when you plan to count anything

## Ethnography — and its limits

- Three commitments (**Blomberg et al.**): the **member's point of view**, **descriptive** not prescriptive, **holistic** — include whatever *members* treat as relevant
- Membership takes time: **Barrett et al. (2004)** logged 100+ hours with sysadmins to see how one engineer's misunderstanding contaminated an entire team's troubleshooting
- **Rapid ethnography** (**Millen, 2000**): immersion only as long as it must be — narrower scope, multiple observers, key informants
- Ethics sharpen in the field: covert observation may be illegal, pseudonyms and note security are non-negotiable, and vulnerable groups may be reachable *only* this way

::: {.callout-warning title="Not so fast... must fieldwork end in 'implications for design'?"}
- The practitioner default: fieldwork earns its cost by producing takeaway bullets designers can act on — rapid ethnography exists precisely to speed this up (**Millen, 2000**)
- **Dourish (2006)**, *Implications for Design*, countered: judging ethnography by its bullet list misreads what it's for — the analytic understanding *is* the contribution, and compressing it blunts the work
- Current consensus: the chapter's reframe — don't ask "should we do field research?", ask "can we succeed without it?"
- Design takeaway: budget for translation — the representations we cover next week (personas, models, journey maps) are the bridge from thick description to design decision
:::

# Discussions

## Can AI-simulated "synthetic users" replace interviews?

Vendors now sell LLM personas you can "interview" in minutes for the price of an API call.

*This is a live commercial reality, not a thought experiment — and it collides head-on with everything this week said about tacit knowledge, the say–do gap, and first-person experience. An LLM has read a million users' words but has never had a Tuesday. If interviews exist to access felt experience, what exactly is a synthetic user giving you — and is it better or worse than the designer's own imagination it replaces?*

## If users adapt to anything valuable, why fund user research at all?

Norman says human-centered design can produce incoherent systems, and history's best tools were never user-tested.

*This attacks the week's founding axiom with the field's own founding father. The violin, the piano, and vi were iterated, not researched — yet the graveyard of products built on founder intuition (see: this week's case study) is vast. Where exactly is the line between healthy skepticism of user signals and the arrogance that costs $1.75 billion?*

## Defining "the user" is a political act — so who should get to do it?

Every target-audience profile includes some people and quietly excludes others.

*The chapter says user-centered design should "fight the urge to design for managers or oneself," but someone still writes the profile — and profiles have budgets attached. Extreme users gave us the tape recorder; ignoring them gives us systems illiterate Uber drivers must rote-learn. Is inclusive sampling an ethical duty, a business strategy, or a luxury for teams with slack?*

## If people can't accurately report their own behavior, is covert observation justified?

The say–do gap says asking fails; consent changes behavior; covert watching solves both — and violates something.

*This puts two of the week's principles in direct conflict: methodological validity (reactivity corrupts data) versus research ethics (people deserve to know they're being studied). Public-space video, virtual-world lurking, and log analysis all live in this gray zone. Where does legitimate unobtrusive research end and surveillance begin?*

# Activities

## Activity 1: The question clinic (~35 min)

**Task** — In groups of 3–4: you're given a brief (a grocery chain wants to understand how families plan weekly meals, to inform a new app). Draft an interview guide: 2 themes, 4 main questions, 2 planned follow-ups each. Then swap guides with another group and red-team theirs: hunt for leading, double-barreled, future-hypothetical, judgmental, and "why"-trap questions.

**Produce** — A markup table with at least 6 rows: flawed question → named flaw (chapter vocabulary) → rewritten version. Plus one forced position: identify one interviewing "rule" from today's lecture your group thinks is wrong or overstated, with a two-sentence argument.

**Time** — 15 min writing · 10 min red-teaming the other group's guide · 10 min share-out

**Debrief** — Which flaw survived your own drafting and was only caught by the other group — and why did it feel like a good question when you wrote it?

## Activity 2: Contextual inquiry of AI use (~40 min)

**Task** — In groups of 3–4: one member (the "master") performs a real task they actually need to do using an AI assistant — drafting an email, debugging code, planning a trip. One member runs a contextual inquiry as the apprentice (context, partnership, interpretation, focus); the rest take structured field notes using Spradley dimensions. Rotate roles once if time allows.

**Produce** — An annotated observation sheet with at least 5 concrete observations, each tagged with a chapter concept (tacit knowledge, say–do gap, context, reactivity, workaround...). Plus one forced position: name one finding that would *not* have surfaced in a plain sit-down interview, and argue why.

**Time** — 25 min inquiry + notes (split across rotations) · 15 min share-out

**Debrief** — What tacit prompting practices did the "master" have that they could not articulate until you asked "show me"?
